content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes some tricks for improving JEM. First, it proposes to replace the original MLE update by importance sampling with the assumption that the samples are from uniform distribution. Second, it proposes to replace negative samples partially with positive samples in the mini-batch. Experimental results show that the method improves the classification accuracy of JEM on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
- The problem of stablizing training of JEM studied by this paper, or in broader context, stablizing training of EBMs, is a fundamental problem and worthwhile to resolve. 

### Weakness
- Unfortunately, this paper is poorly writing. 
  - It misses a lot of important references in the literature of EBMs and contrastive divergence. 
  - The presentation is confusing. For example, in section 4.2, the idea of including data point in negative samples has been repeatedly introduced twice without clear logic connection. There're also minor writing errors here and there, such as undeleted writing comment at the end of section 2 and missing reference to Appendix in section 4.2.
  - The description of proposed methods and implementation is unclear. For example, I don't really understand how it could be possible to not include any negative samples in Eqn. 19 and why it is reasonable to do that. 
- The proposed method is problematic in principle.
  - Estimating MI with $p_{data}$ instead of $p_\theta$ is not well-motivated. Even if samples from $p_{data}$ is completely a subset of $p_\theta$ (this assumption made by the paper is also pretty shaky), they could still be two totally different distributions. 
  - The proposed objective with importance sampling will in principle converge to a different density function than the target EBM except for a very special case. 
  - I fail to get why it makes sense to include real samples to the estimation of model statistics. 
- Experimental results are weak.
  - First, it it a bad practice to include all experimental results in appendix, which means us reviewers can completely ignore those results when evaluating the paper. 
  - According to the results, only from the perspective of accuracy the proposed method performs slight better than JEM. No other metrics like FID or inception score has been reported to valid that there's at least no degradation to the generative performance. Also, calibration is worse compared to JEM according to ECE.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity is bad and I had a hard time understanding what the actual proposed method is, why it makes sense and how it is implemented in practice.

Quality is weak as the proposed method is not valid in principle. 

The proposed method is based on classic importance sampling and mutual information. Though novel variants of those methods have been proposed. The new variants haven't been fully justified.

I don't see enough implementation details to reproduce the results.
content.summary_of_the_review: The problem that this paper proposes to resolve is principled and worthwhile to explore. However, the paper needs a major improvement on the presentation of the method, theoretical justification as well as empirical results.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors investigate the use of training data points (both exclusively, and in combination with SGLD samples) to more effectively train joint EBMs (JEMS), which are well known to be difficult to train. The incorporation of a mutual information term into the training objective is also considered, as is a model combination approach.

The current manuscript is very much in an "in-progress" state, with incomplete sections, notes about finishing them, and all results currently relegated to the appendix.

While the core arguments of the paper seem clear, the paper is not yet coherent enough to be considered for publication at ICLR 2023, and requires a major revision. I look forward to it.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- The paper argues for "anchoring" denominator stats normally from model samples with training data, and shows the best results on cifar10,100 (table 1 and 2) by relying solely on training data, which is interesting.

Limitations:

- As elaborated in the summary, the paper is in an in-progress state, and not ready to be considered for publication.

Other comments:

- The approach seems quite related to supervised variants of InfoNCE. This perspective may assist the authors in revising and
 finalizing their paper for a future conference.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose ways to stabilize the training of Joint Energy-based Model (JEM). In the method,  mutual information between inputs x and label y is added in the previous objective. The author claim that it will be more stable for training. And they show the effectiveness of the proposed method on CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and speech tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Good background introduction. Nice written with lot of explanation. It is easy for other to follow.
2. The authors shows the effective of the proposed methods on several tasks. Not only CIFAR10, CIFAR100, but also include a harder task speech ASR task.


Weaknesses:

1. It seem unclear whey the previous training method is unstable. No examples are shown in the paper. The authors say "In fact, the authors declared that the training instability was the most significant flaw of the proposed model.". Is the reason is the unstable of SGLD samples? The motivation could be hard understood by readers.

2. In the proposed method, one extra is included. Equation (19) is used for training. However, generated SGLD samples are used. And importance sampling is also used in Equation (20). Both of these two operation increase the destabilization. This seems not fit the title of the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: This is a well written paper. However, the novelty and contribution seem not solid.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a series of improvements over Joint Energy-based Models (JEM) -- which reinterpret classifiers as Energy-Based Models (EBM), providing them with generative ability as well as a number of other benefits such as improved calibration, OOD detection, semi-supervised training objectives and adversarial robustness. JEMs have nice properties when trained, but their training procedure is notoriously unstable and difficult to tune. This has limited the application of these models mainly to domains where EBMs have been highly tuned (such as images). 

This paper presents improvements to the JEM training procedure by [EXPLAIN WHAT THEY DO] by rescaling the negative sample gradients using self-normalized importance sampling and adding a mutual information regularizer. Effectively, this regularizer equates to generating negative samples from p(x|y) instead of p(x). 

These improvements together lead to notable improvements in results. Accuracy improves over the original work's results as well as calibration. As well, these stability improvements enable JEM to be applied to audio data. Here we observe the same types of improvements presented in the original JEM work but in this domain the original JEM training procedure fails to train the models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

The parts of this paper that are complete are well written. I really enjoyed the intuition given to motivate the proposed stability improvements. I found this helped reinforce the equations and improved my understanding. The results (which are all in the appendix) demonstrated an improvement over the original JEM.


Weaknesses:

There are a number of clear issues with this paper. First, the results are not presented in the main body. Page limits are difficult to work around but encourage concision, simplicity, and clarity. All content necessary to evaluate the work should be in the main body. Its fine to place additional results in the appendix but the main results should be in the main paper. Besides this there are notes to the author still in the paper in a few places as well as a few dead links. 

Besides these issues, there are no experimental details given (in the main paper or appendix) so the work is not necessarily reproducible. Also, in my experience self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS) can be very difficult to use and have almost 0 effective sample size. If the method is to be based on SNIS, you should provide some evidence that the ESS is reasonable.

content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The parts of the work that are complete are indeed well written, but overall this is not a completed paper. There are no experimental details and the results are all in the appendix. There are no evaluations besides classification and ECE. There is no indication that the SNIS procedure actually does what it's supposed to. 

The paper is clearly not reproducible since the architectures and training details are not explained.
content.summary_of_the_review: The ideas presented in this paper are interesting and of general interest to the community. Unfortunately, the work is not completed. I was initially excited to read this paper because of its interesting method and high quality results but it's not finished and should not be accepted.

content.title: Stabilized training of joint energy-based models and its practical applications
content.TL;DR: JEM with stabilized training using SGLD samples; it enables us to apply it to speech
content.abstract: The recently proposed Joint Energy-based Model (JEM) interprets discriminatively trained classifier p(y|x) as an energy model, which is also trained as a generative model describing the distribution of the input observations p(x). The JEM training relies on "positive examples" (i.e. examples from the training data set) as well as on "negative examples", which are samples from the modeled distribution p(x) generated by means of Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD). Unfortunately, SGLD often fails to deliver negative samples of sufficient quality during the standard JEM training, which causes a very unbalanced contribution from the positive and negative examples when calculating gradients for JEM updates. As a consequence, the standard JEM training is quite unstable requiring careful tuning of hyper-parameters and frequent restarts when the training starts diverging. This makes it difficult to apply JEM to different neural network architectures, modalities, and tasks. In this work, we propose a training procedure that stabilizes SGLD-based JEM training (ST-JEM) by balancing the contribution from the positive and negative examples. We also propose to add an additional "regularization" term to the training objective -- MI between the input observations x and output labels y -- which encourages the JEM classifier to make more certain decisions about output labels. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 tasks. We also consider the task of classifying phonemes in a speech signal, for which we were not able to train JEM without the proposed stabilization. We show that a convincing speech can be generated from the trained model. Alternatively, corrupted speech can be de-noised by bringing it closer to the modeled speech distribution using a few SGLD iterations. We also propose and discuss additional applications of the trained model.
